results.blind_working: Displacement = final - initial = -6 - 4 = -10 m.
Path length = 8 + 11 = 19 m. Displacement = -3 - 0 = -3 m.
Motion is relative: the passenger's position is fixed in the train frame but changes in the platform frame.
On a closed path the displacement is zero, but the path length is not zero, so A is false. R is the correct definition of displacement, so R is true.

I: |displacement| equals path length for motion in one direction without reversal, which can be the negative direction too, so I is incorrect. II: In 1D, path length exceeds |displacement| only if the direction reverses, so II is correct.
Velocity is the slope of the x-t graph: (14 - 2)/(4 - 0) = 3 m/s.
Velocity falls uniformly, so it is zero at t = 2 s. Distance = 1/2·2·10 + 1/2·2·10 = 20 m. Displacement is 0 but distance is 20 m.
Change in velocity = area under a-t graph = 3·4 + (-2)·2 = 8. Final velocity = 2 + 8 = 10 m/s.
x-t slope gives velocity, v-t slope gives acceleration, v-t area gives displacement, a-t area gives change in velocity. So A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

A true (constant x means rest). B false (v-t is a straight line for uniform acceleration). C true (concave up means positive acceleration). D true (v changes sign where it crosses the axis). E false (signed area gives displacement, not distance). So A, C, D.
Acceleration is zero only if velocity (magnitude and direction) is constant. Constant speed with changing direction still gives acceleration.
54 km/h = 15 m/s; 2 min = 120 s; motion is along a straight line in one direction, so displacement = 15 × 120 = 1800 m.
A is true: the direction of velocity changes, so there is centripetal acceleration. R is true: constant velocity means constant magnitude. But R does not explain A.

I is correct, e.g. uniform circular motion. II: a change in velocity direction means velocity is not constant, so the motion is accelerated, i.e. non-uniform in the constant-velocity sense. This depends on the convention that uniform motion means constant velocity, so II is judged correct.
Total distance is 120 + 80 = 200 m. Total time is 20 s. Average speed = 200/20 = 10 m/s.
For equal distances, average speed is the harmonic mean: 2·30·60/(30+60) = 3600/90 = 40 km/h.
The particle turns at t = 2 s, where x = -1. Also x(0) = 3 and x(5) = 8. Distance = |(-1) - 3| + |8 - (-1)| = 4 + 9 = 13 m. Average speed = 13/5 = 2.6 m/s.
A: equal distances give 2·20·30/50 = 24 m/s (III). B: equal times give (20+30)/2 = 25 m/s (IV). C: displacement is 0, so average velocity is 0 (I). D: 200 m/10 s = 20 m/s (II).

A is true because distance ≥ |displacement|. B is true. C is false: average velocity is zero for a round trip, not average speed. D is true by definition. E is false: after a reversal, distance exceeds |displacement|, so average speed is larger. Correct set is A, B and D.
At the top v = 0, so h = u²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m.
Distance in nth second is s_n = u + a(n - 1/2) = 0 + 4(4.5) = 18 m.
Stopping distance s = v²/(2a), so s ∝ v². Doubling the speed (10 to 20 m/s) quadruples s: 4 × 10 = 40 m.
At the top v = 0 but acceleration is still g downward, so A is false and R is true.
I: s ∝ t², so s(2) : s(4) − s(2) = 4 : 12 = 1:3, not 1:2, so I is incorrect. II: a = v dv/dx = 3x·3 = 9x, which is not constant, so II is incorrect.
Momentum p = mv has both magnitude and direction and adds by the vector law, so it is a vector. Energy and temperature are scalars, and current is a scalar.
Currents meeting at a junction add algebraically and do not follow the triangle law of vector addition, so current is a scalar.
|λA| = |−3| × 5 = 15 units. The negative sign reverses the direction, so the result points opposite to A.

Equal vectors: same magnitude, same direction (A-III). Negative vector: same magnitude, opposite direction (B-I). Null vector: zero magnitude, arbitrary direction (C-II). Current: has direction but adds algebraically (D-IV).

A true: a free vector is unchanged by parallel shift. B false: pressure is a scalar. C true: a null vector has zero magnitude and indeterminate direction. D false: work is a dot product, hence a scalar. E true: multiplying by −2 doubles the magnitude and reverses the direction. Correct set is A, C, E.
The forces are perpendicular, so R = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 N.
R^2 = P^2 + P^2 + 2P^2 cos(theta) = P^2, so 2 + 2cos(theta) = 1, giving cos(theta) = -1/2 and theta = 120 degrees.
Change in velocity = v_final - v_initial = 5j - 5i. Its magnitude is 5*sqrt(2) m/s and it points north-west.
The resultant must lie between |5 - 3| = 2 N and 5 + 3 = 8 N. Since 10 N is outside this range, A is true. R is the general rule and directly explains A.

I: three forces are in equilibrium if their magnitudes can form a triangle. 4 + 6 = 10 >= 9, so they can, and I is correct. II: |A+B|^2 = |A-B|^2 gives 4 A.B = 0, so A.B = 0 and the vectors are perpendicular. II is correct.
A×B = (2×4 − 1×1) k̂ = 7k̂; area = ½|A×B| = 3.5 square units
î×ĵ = k̂, and î×k̂ = −ĵ
ĵ×k̂ = î (III); k̂×ĵ = −î (IV); î·î = 1 (II); î×î = 0 (I)

A and B are true (A×B is perpendicular to both A and B). C is false because A×B = −B×A. D is false: both being zero would need sinθ = cosθ = 0, which is impossible. E is true since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. So A, B and E only.
|A| = √(9+16) = 5, so the unit vector is (3î+4ĵ)/5.
A·B = 6+12 = 18 and |B| = 5, so the component is 18/5 = 3.6.
A component equals A cosθ, which can never exceed A. So A is false and R is true.
I: magnitude = √(4+1+4) = 3, so the unit vector is correct, and direction cosines squared always sum to 1. II: (2+1)/√2 = 3/√2, correct. Both correct.
Opposite directions, so the speeds add: 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 90 × 5/18 = 25 m/s.
To land directly opposite, the swimmer heads upstream so the drift cancels. Speed across = √(25 − 9) = 4 m/s, so t = 120/4 = 30 s.
Rain relative to the man has components 6 down and 2√3 toward him from the front. tanθ = 2√3/6 = 1/√3, so θ = 30° from the vertical, tilted forward.

A is true. B is true: both have acceleration g, so relative acceleration is zero. C is false: zero drift needs swimmer speed greater than river speed. D is true, reading u as river speed and v as swimmer speed. E is false: the umbrella should follow the rain's direction relative to the man.
v = dr/dt = 3i + 4t j. At t = 2 s this gives v = 3i + 8j m/s.
x = 4t and y = (1/2)(2)t^2 = t^2. Substituting t = x/4 gives y = x^2/16.
A is true: in curved motion, acceleration need not be along velocity. R is false: the perpendicular component changes direction only, not speed.
v = 2i + (4-2t)j, so at t = 2 s, v = 2i, which is not zero; I is false. a = -2j, which is perpendicular to 2i; II is true.
Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g = 2×20×0.5/10 = 2 s.
Fall time t = √(2h/g) = √(2×45/10) = 3 s. Horizontal distance x = 15×3 = 45 m.
A: speed at top = u cosθ (II). B: acceleration at top = g (III). C: H = u²sin²45°/2g = u²/4g (IV). D: R_max = u²/g (I). So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

A true: sin2θ is the same for complementary angles. B true: at the top, velocity is horizontal and g is vertical. C true: KE at top = ½m(u cosθ)² = K cos²θ. D false: fall time √(2h/g) does not depend on horizontal speed. E false: R = 4H cotθ, so R = H needs tanθ = 4, not 45°. Correct set is A, B, C.
In 2 s the velocity turns through (2/12)*360° = 60°. |Δv| = 2v sin(30°) = 2*10*0.5 = 10 m s^-1
Speed is constant, so KE is constant: A is true. Centripetal acceleration has constant magnitude but its direction keeps changing, so it is not a constant vector: R is false.
I: a = ω^2 r with ω the same, so 2r gives double, not four times: I is incorrect. II: over half a revolution, displacement = 2r and time = πr/v, so average velocity = 2v/π ≠ v: II is incorrect.
